answerKey.primaryProblem: Pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis of the right index finger (positive Kanavel's signs) following a barbed-wire laceration 3 days ago - a surgical emergency
differential: Pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis (most likely given all 4 Kanavel signs)
Simple cellulitis of the finger (would not typically cause fusiform swelling, flexed posture, or sheath tenderness along full length)
Felon (pulp space abscess - usually localized to fingertip, not whole-finger fusiform swelling)
Septic arthritis of a finger joint (more joint-localized, less diffuse)
Herpetic whitlow (vesicular, less likely post-mechanical injury, no systemic fever typically)
keyFindings: All four Kanavel signs positive: fusiform swelling, flexed resting posture, tenderness along flexor sheath, pain with passive extension
Low-grade fever 38.0 C and tachycardia 96 bpm consistent with early systemic response
Mechanism: penetrating barbed-wire injury 3 days ago with delayed/inadequate wound care (water rinse only)
No spreading cellulitis/lymphangitic streaking yet, but infection is sheath-contained and can progress to tendon necrosis rapidly
Tetanus booster overdue (last dose ~10 years ago, booster recommended at 10 years for clean wound but this is a contaminated wound requiring booster if >5 years)
plan: Do NOT delay care with a phone-in oral antibiotic prescription alone - this presentation requires same-day in-person evaluation

Immediately contact supervising physician to discuss and arrange urgent in-person surgical/hand evaluation (ideally today) given risk of tendon sheath necrosis and need for possible surgical drainage/irrigation
Arrange transport or direct patient to nearest emergency department or hand surgeon today; explain the 80-mile distance does not change the urgency - delay risks permanent loss of hand function
Advise against attempting to 'work through it' during calving season; functional loss of the finger is a real risk if untreated 24-48 more hours
Administer or arrange tetanus booster (Tdap) given contaminated wound and >5 years since last dose, at the facility he is referred to
Document discussion of urgency and patient's reluctance/understanding clearly in the chart
Do not initiate IV or empiric broad antibiotics via telehealth alone without the in-person surgical evaluation; this is beyond independent telehealth management for this condition
redFlags: Fusiform 'sausage' swelling of the entire finger
Finger held in flexed position at rest
Tenderness along the full length of the flexor tendon sheath
Pain with passive extension of the finger
Fever and tachycardia suggesting systemic involvement
Delay beyond 24-48 hours risking tendon necrosis and permanent loss of function
educationPoints: Kanavel's four signs are a classic bedside/telehealth-adaptable exam for flexor tenosynovitis and can be assessed via guided camera exam and patient self-palpation
Flexor tenosynovitis is a surgical emergency - oral antibiotics alone are not adequate treatment, even if the patient's convenience and distance to care are compelling
Barbed-wire and other puncture/laceration injuries from livestock environments carry contamination risk including atypical and polymicrobial organisms
Tetanus prophylaxis should be reassessed with any contaminated wound; a 10-year-old booster is not sufficient for a dirty/contaminated wound (5-year threshold applies)
Rural/distance barriers must be explicitly addressed in the plan (transport, timing) rather than allowing them to drive under-treatment
PA students must recognize when a presentation exceeds safe telehealth management scope and requires immediate escalation and in-person care

facts.chart: 3-day history of right index finger pain and swelling after barbed-wire cut, requesting antibiotics called in
facts.says: Cut my finger on some barbed wire three days ago fixing fence. It's gotten pretty swollen and sore. I was hoping you could just call in some antibiotics so I don't have to drive in - we're right in the middle of calving.

facts.chart: Laceration to palmar aspect of right index finger from barbed wire while repairing fence
facts.says: Snagged it reaching through a fence line. Wire caught me right across the palm side of my pointer finger.

facts.chart: Wound cleaned with water only; no antiseptic, no medical attention sought at time of injury
facts.says: Just rinsed it off with water from the hose and wrapped a bandana around it. Didn't think much of it at the time.

facts.chart: Swelling and pain have progressively worsened over 3 days; now unable to fully straighten the finger
facts.says: First day it was just a little sore. By yesterday it was swelling up and today I can barely bend or straighten it without it really hurting.

facts.chart: Sharp pain with attempted finger extension; dull ache at rest
facts.says: It's a dull ache most of the time, but if I try to straighten it out it's a sharp, bad pain.

facts.chart: Patient reports finger stays curled; difficult to voluntarily straighten
facts.says: It just wants to stay curled up. I have to really fight it to get it to straighten, and that's when it hurts the worst.

facts.chart: Subjective fever and chills over past 24 hours
facts.says: Felt kind of hot and shivery yesterday evening. Took my temperature this morning and it was up a bit.

facts.chart: Unable to grip tools or rope effectively with right hand due to pain
facts.says: Can't really grip my rope or the fencing pliers right now, it hurts too much. That's a real problem with calving going on.

facts.chart: Denies redness tracking up the hand or arm
facts.says: No, it's just the finger that's red and puffy, not creeping up my hand or arm as far as I can tell.

facts.chart: Denies pus or drainage from the wound
facts.says: No pus or anything coming out of it, just looks swollen and shiny.

facts.chart: Denies numbness or tingling in the finger
facts.says: No, I can still feel everything fine, it just hurts.

facts.chart: Denies nausea, vomiting, confusion, or feeling generally unwell beyond local symptoms
facts.says: Other than the chills, I feel pretty normal otherwise. No throwing up or anything.

facts.chart: No history of diabetes mellitus
facts.says: No, never been told I have diabetes or anything like that.

facts.chart: No immunosuppressive conditions or medications
facts.says: I'm healthy otherwise, don't take anything regular.

facts.chart: No prior infections or injuries to this hand
facts.says: Never had trouble with this hand before, this is a first.

facts.chart: Occasional ibuprofen 200-400mg PRN for muscle soreness; no other medications
facts.says: Just ibuprofen now and then when my back's sore from work. Nothing else.

facts.chart: No known drug allergies
facts.says: No allergies that I know of.

facts.chart: Last tetanus-containing vaccine was Tdap at age 16, approximately 10 years ago, during a school vaccination program
facts.says: Tetanus shot? I think I got one back in high school, maybe sophomore year. Haven't had one since that I remember.

facts.chart: Works as a ranch hand on a cattle ranch roughly 80 miles from the nearest clinic in eastern Montana
facts.says: I work the cattle ranch out here. Nearest clinic is about an hour and a half drive, more if the roads are bad.

facts.chart: Currently in calving season, a critical and labor-intensive period; reluctant to leave work
facts.says: Calving season, man, this is the worst time to be laid up. We're short-handed as it is.

facts.chart: Minimizes severity of symptoms; prefers phone-in prescription over in-person visit
facts.says: I don't need to make the whole trip in for this, do I? Can't you just call something in?

facts.chart: Patient downplays pain severity; tends to minimize discomfort to avoid appearing weak
facts.says: It's not that bad, I've dealt with worse. I can tough it out.

facts.chart: Has access to a personal truck; driving itself is not a logistical barrier, time away from work is the main concern
facts.says: I've got my truck, getting there isn't the issue, it's just the time away that's rough.

facts.chart: Has basic health insurance through ranch employer but worried about cost of an ER visit or missed work pay
facts.says: I've got insurance through the ranch, but I don't know what an ER visit runs, and if I'm not working, I'm not getting paid.

facts.chart: Drinks 2-3 beers on weekends, denies daily use
facts.says: Have a couple beers on the weekend sometimes, nothing crazy.

facts.chart: Uses chewing tobacco occasionally, about once a day
facts.says: I dip sometimes, maybe once a day.

facts.chart: No family history of diabetes, bleeding disorders, or immune conditions
facts.says: Nobody in my family has diabetes or anything like that that I know of.

facts.chart: No other recent cuts or animal bites besides the barbed wire injury
facts.says: Nope, just this one cut from the fence, nothing else recent.

facts.chart: Has been applying over-the-counter triple antibiotic ointment since day 2
facts.says: Been putting some of that triple antibiotic ointment on it since yesterday, figured that'd help.

facts.chart: Patient's stated goal is to get antibiotics without an in-person visit so he can keep working through calving season
facts.says: Honestly I just want something to knock this out quick so I can get back to work. I really don't want to lose a whole day.

facts.chart: Patient does not realize the finger findings could represent a surgical emergency; believes it is a routine infected cut
facts.says: I figured it's just infected and needs some antibiotics, like any other cut that goes bad.

facts.chart: When told of the urgency, expresses surprise and concern about work but ultimately willing to consider going in if clearly necessary
facts.says: Wait, really, it's that serious? ...I guess if it's gonna cost me my finger working right, I'd rather go in. Just didn't realize it was that bad.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient believes his last tetanus shot was in high school, roughly 10 years ago, and is uncertain of the exact timing
mismatches.recordEvidence: Immunization record confirms Tdap given at age 16 (approximately 10 years ago) with no subsequent doses, matching the patient's recollection but confirming it exceeds the 5-year threshold for a contaminated wound
mismatches.teachingPoint: Even when the patient's memory and the record agree, learners must still apply the correct clinical threshold (5 years for contaminated/dirty wounds, not the routine 10-year interval) rather than assuming an old booster is sufficient.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient insists this is a routine infected cut that just needs a phone-in antibiotic, downplaying severity
mismatches.recordEvidence: Today's vitals show fever (38.0 C) and tachycardia (96 bpm) with physical exam findings (fusiform swelling, flexed posture, sheath tenderness, pain on passive extension) all documented as positive, reflecting a surgical emergency rather than a simple infected laceration
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patient self-assessment of severity can be inaccurate, especially in those who minimize pain; objective exam and vital sign findings must guide triage decisions, not the patient's own framing of the problem.

objectives.text: Elicit a focused history of a penetrating hand injury including mechanism, wound care, symptom progression, and systemic symptoms (fever/chills), then obtain vital signs
Perform and correctly interpret a remote camera-based and patient-guided exam to identify all four Kanavel signs of flexor tenosynovitis
Differentiate flexor tenosynovitis from simple cellulitis or felon by checking for spreading redness, drainage, and the full constellation of exam findings
Assess tetanus immunization status against the correct booster interval for a contaminated wound and identify the mismatch between a seemingly adequate history and the actual clinical threshold
Recognize when a presentation exceeds the scope of telehealth management and requires same-day in-person surgical evaluation, overriding the patient's preference for a phone-in prescription
Address social and logistical barriers (distance, work demands during calving season, cost concerns) while still conveying the urgency of escalation to the supervising physician and in-person care

scenario.studentBrief: You are a PA student on a telehealth rotation in primary/urgent care. Tyler Brandt, a 26-year-old ranch hand calling from a rural property in eastern Montana, is requesting a phone-in antibiotic prescription for a finger he cut on barbed wire 3 days ago. Conduct a focused history and remote exam, and determine the appropriate next step.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Right index finger pain and swelling after a barbed-wire cut 3 days ago, with patient requesting antibiotics called in
scenario.openingLine: Hey, thanks for calling me back. I cut my finger on some barbed wire a few days ago and it's gotten pretty swollen and sore - was hoping you could just call in some antibiotics so I don't have to make the drive in. We're right in the middle of calving season.
tasks: Obtain a focused history of the injury, wound care, and symptom progression
Perform a guided remote exam of the finger and hand
Review the patient's tetanus immunization status and determine if a booster is indicated
Assess the severity of the infection and determine whether phone-in antibiotics are appropriate
Formulate a management plan and escalate to the supervising physician as needed

profile.summary: A 26-year-old rural ranch hand presents by telehealth 3 days after a barbed-wire laceration to the palmar index finger, requesting a phone-in antibiotic prescription to avoid missing work during calving season. Guided remote examination reveals all four Kanavel signs, teaching PA students to recognize pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis as a surgical emergency requiring same-day in-person evaluation and escalation, despite the patient's minimization of symptoms and real logistical barriers.
profile.title: Finger Swelling After a Barbed-Wire Cut in a Rural Ranch Hand: Recognizing Flexor Tenosynovitis by Telehealth
